---
title: "RNNs and LSTMs"
---

## Why Sequence Models Need State

An ordinary feed-forward network maps each input independently:

$$
y_t=f(x_t).
$$

A recurrent neural network maintains a hidden state that summarizes the prefix:

$$
h_t=f(x_t,h_{t-1}),
\qquad
y_t=g(h_t).
$$

The same parameters are reused at every time step. This gives an RNN:

- a variable-length input interface
- parameter sharing across positions
- an inductive bias toward sequential processing
- a fixed-size state through which past information must flow

## Vanilla RNN

The standard tanh RNN is

$$
a_t=W_{xh}x_t+W_{hh}h_{t-1}+b_h,
$$

$$
h_t=\tanh(a_t),
$$

$$
y_t=W_{hy}h_t+b_y.
$$

The initial state $h_0$ may be zero, learned, or provided by another encoder.

### Model structure

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    X1[Input x₁] --> C1[RNN cell]
    H0[Initial state h₀] --> C1
    C1 --> H1[Hidden state h₁]
    H1 --> C2[RNN cell]
    X2[Input x₂] --> C2
    C2 --> H2[Hidden state h₂]
    H2 --> C3[RNN cell]
    X3[Input x₃] --> C3
    C3 --> H3[Hidden state h₃]

    H1 --> Y1[Output y₁]
    H2 --> Y2[Output y₂]
    H3 --> Y3[Output y₃]

    classDef state fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4c78a8,color:#222;
    classDef cell fill:#f3e8ff,stroke:#8b5cf6,color:#222;
    classDef input fill:#e8f8ee,stroke:#3a8f5c,color:#222;
    class H0,H1,H2,H3 state;
    class C1,C2,C3 cell;
    class X1,X2,X3 input;
```

The three cells above are copies of the **same computation with shared
parameters**, not three independently learned layers. Drawing the recurrence
across time is called **unrolling** the RNN.

### Tensor shapes

For batch size $B$, sequence length $T$, input size $d_x$, hidden size $d_h$,
and output size $d_y$:

| Tensor | Shape |
|---|---:|
| Input sequence $X$ | $(B,T,d_x)$ |
| Hidden state $h_t$ | $(B,d_h)$ |
| Input weight $W_{xh}$ | $(d_h,d_x)$ |
| Recurrent weight $W_{hh}$ | $(d_h,d_h)$ |
| Output sequence $Y$ | $(B,T,d_y)$ |

### Minimal PyTorch implementation

```{python}
import torch
import torch.nn as nn


class SimpleRNNCell(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.input_proj = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size, bias=True)
        self.hidden_proj = nn.Linear(hidden_size, hidden_size, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x_t, h_previous):
        return torch.tanh(
            self.input_proj(x_t) + self.hidden_proj(h_previous)
        )


class SimpleRNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.cell = SimpleRNNCell(input_size, hidden_size)

    def forward(self, inputs, initial_state=None):
        batch_size, _, _ = inputs.shape
        if initial_state is None:
            hidden = inputs.new_zeros(batch_size, self.hidden_size)
        else:
            hidden = initial_state

        outputs = []
        for x_t in inputs.unbind(dim=1):
            hidden = self.cell(x_t, hidden)
            outputs.append(hidden)

        return torch.stack(outputs, dim=1), hidden


torch.manual_seed(0)
sequence = torch.randn(2, 5, 3)
rnn = SimpleRNN(input_size=3, hidden_size=7)
all_hidden_states, final_hidden_state = rnn(sequence)

assert all_hidden_states.shape == (2, 5, 7)
assert final_hidden_state.shape == (2, 7)
```

## Backpropagation Through Time

Unrolling converts recurrence into a deep computation graph whose depth grows
with sequence length. Training differentiates through this graph, which is
called **backpropagation through time** (BPTT).

For the vanilla RNN,

$$
\frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_{t-1}}
=
\operatorname{diag}\left(1-\tanh^2(a_t)\right)W_{hh}.
$$

A gradient traveling from time $T$ to time $t$ contains a product of Jacobians:

$$
\frac{\partial h_T}{\partial h_t}
=
\prod_{k=t+1}^{T}
\frac{\partial h_k}{\partial h_{k-1}}.
$$

Repeated multiplication causes:

- **vanishing gradients** when the relevant singular values are mostly below 1
- **exploding gradients** when they are mostly above 1

Tanh saturation further shrinks gradients because
$1-\tanh^2(a_t)\approx0$ for large $|a_t|$.

### Practical mitigations

- gradient clipping for exploding gradients
- orthogonal or carefully scaled recurrent initialization
- truncated BPTT to limit graph length and memory
- gated cells such as LSTMs and GRUs
- skip connections and normalization in recurrent architectures

Truncated BPTT bounds training cost, but it also prevents gradients from
directly assigning credit across truncation boundaries.

## Long Short-Term Memory

An LSTM introduces a cell state $c_t$ with an additive update path. Three gates
control what to forget, write, and expose.

For concatenated input

$$
z_t=[x_t;h_{t-1}],
$$

the gates and candidate memory are

$$
f_t=\sigma(W_fz_t+b_f)
\qquad\text{forget gate},
$$

$$
i_t=\sigma(W_iz_t+b_i)
\qquad\text{input gate},
$$

$$
o_t=\sigma(W_oz_t+b_o)
\qquad\text{output gate},
$$

$$
\widetilde c_t=\tanh(W_cz_t+b_c)
\qquad\text{candidate memory}.
$$

The cell and hidden states update as

$$
\boxed{c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot\widetilde c_t},
$$

$$
\boxed{h_t=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t)}.
$$

### LSTM cell structure

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    C0[Previous cell cₜ₋₁] --> MULF((×))
    XH[Input xₜ and hidden hₜ₋₁] --> F[Forget gate fₜ = sigmoid]
    XH --> I[Input gate iₜ = sigmoid]
    XH --> G[Candidate c̃ₜ = tanh]
    XH --> O[Output gate oₜ = sigmoid]

    F --> MULF
    I --> MULI((×))
    G --> MULI
    MULF --> ADD((+))
    MULI --> ADD
    ADD --> C1[New cell state cₜ]

    C1 --> TANH[tanh]
    TANH --> MULO((×))
    O --> MULO
    MULO --> H1[New hidden state hₜ]

    classDef state fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4c78a8,color:#222;
    classDef gate fill:#fff2cc,stroke:#c49a00,color:#222;
    classDef candidate fill:#e8f8ee,stroke:#3a8f5c,color:#222;
    classDef op fill:#f3e8ff,stroke:#8b5cf6,color:#222;
    class C0,C1,H1 state;
    class F,I,O gate;
    class G,TANH candidate;
    class MULF,MULI,MULO,ADD op;
```

The upper cell-state path is the key difference from a vanilla RNN. It combines
old memory and new content **additively**, while sigmoid gates provide
element-wise control.

### Why the LSTM helps gradient flow

Holding the gates fixed for intuition,

$$
\frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}}=f_t.
$$

Across several steps,

$$
\frac{\partial c_T}{\partial c_t}
\approx
\prod_{k=t+1}^{T} f_k.
$$

When forget gates remain near one, the cell provides a nearly linear path for
information and gradients. This avoids repeatedly passing the main memory
through a saturating tanh transformation at every time step.

LSTMs mitigate vanishing gradients; they do not eliminate them. Products of
forget gates below one still decay, and the full gradient includes additional
paths through gate dependencies.

## Minimal LSTM Implementation

Efficient implementations fuse all four affine transformations into one matrix
multiplication:

$$
[f_t,i_t,\widetilde c_t,o_t]
=
W[x_t;h_{t-1}]+b.
$$

```{python}
class MinimalLSTMCell(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.gates = nn.Linear(input_size + hidden_size, 4 * hidden_size)

    def forward(self, x_t, state):
        hidden_previous, cell_previous = state
        combined = torch.cat([x_t, hidden_previous], dim=-1)
        forget_raw, input_raw, candidate_raw, output_raw = self.gates(
            combined
        ).chunk(4, dim=-1)

        forget_gate = torch.sigmoid(forget_raw)
        input_gate = torch.sigmoid(input_raw)
        candidate = torch.tanh(candidate_raw)
        output_gate = torch.sigmoid(output_raw)

        cell = forget_gate * cell_previous + input_gate * candidate
        hidden = output_gate * torch.tanh(cell)
        return hidden, cell


class MinimalLSTM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.cell = MinimalLSTMCell(input_size, hidden_size)

    def forward(self, inputs, initial_state=None):
        batch_size, _, _ = inputs.shape
        if initial_state is None:
            hidden = inputs.new_zeros(batch_size, self.hidden_size)
            cell = inputs.new_zeros(batch_size, self.hidden_size)
        else:
            hidden, cell = initial_state

        outputs = []
        for x_t in inputs.unbind(dim=1):
            hidden, cell = self.cell(x_t, (hidden, cell))
            outputs.append(hidden)

        return torch.stack(outputs, dim=1), (hidden, cell)


lstm = MinimalLSTM(input_size=3, hidden_size=7)
lstm_outputs, (final_hidden, final_cell) = lstm(sequence)

assert lstm_outputs.shape == (2, 5, 7)
assert final_hidden.shape == (2, 7)
assert final_cell.shape == (2, 7)
```

### Parameter count

For input size $d_x$ and hidden size $d_h$, the fused LSTM affine layer has

$$
4d_h(d_x+d_h)+4d_h
$$

parameters. A comparable vanilla RNN has

$$
d_h(d_x+d_h)+d_h.
$$

An LSTM cell therefore has roughly four times the recurrent-cell parameters and
affine compute of a vanilla RNN with the same dimensions.

## Understanding the Gates

| Gate | Range | Multiplies | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Forget $f_t$ | $(0,1)$ | old cell $c_{t-1}$ | retain or erase old memory |
| Input $i_t$ | $(0,1)$ | candidate $\widetilde c_t$ | write new memory |
| Output $o_t$ | $(0,1)$ | exposed $\tanh(c_t)$ | reveal cell information as hidden state |

The cell state is not constrained to $(-1,1)$ because it is an additive
accumulator. The hidden state is bounded by the output gate and tanh.

### Connection to SwiGLU

Both LSTMs and SwiGLU use multiplicative, input-dependent modulation:

$$
\text{content}\odot\text{gate}.
$$

But their roles differ:

| SwiGLU | LSTM |
|---|---|
| gates features within one feed-forward evaluation | gates state flow across time |
| no persistent cell state | maintains $c_t$ across sequence positions |
| SiLU gate can exceed one or become slightly negative | sigmoid gates remain between zero and one |
| increases feature interactions | controls remembering, writing, and reading |

See [Activation Functions](activations.qmd#gated-activations) for the SwiGLU
derivation.

## RNN, LSTM, and Transformer Comparison

| Property | Vanilla RNN | LSTM | Causal Transformer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sequence computation | sequential | sequential | parallel during training/prefill |
| Persistent state | $h_t$ | $h_t$ and $c_t$ | KV cache during decoding |
| Direct path to distant token | through every intermediate state | gated cell path | attention edge |
| Training path length across distance $T$ | $O(T)$ | $O(T)$ | often $O(1)$ per layer with full attention |
| Per-layer sequence cost | $O(T)$ recurrent steps | $O(T)$ recurrent steps | $O(T^2)$ dense attention |
| Streaming memory | fixed state | fixed state | growing cache unless attention is bounded |

RNNs and LSTMs remain attractive for streaming and bounded-state settings.
Transformers dominate many large-scale sequence tasks because training can be
parallelized across positions and attention provides short paths between distant
tokens.

## Common Variants

- **Bidirectional RNN/LSTM:** runs separate recurrences forward and backward;
  useful when the entire sequence is available, but not causal.
- **Stacked RNN/LSTM:** feeds one recurrent layer's sequence into another.
- **GRU:** combines LSTM-style control into reset and update gates with no
  separate cell state.
- **Peephole LSTM:** gates also inspect the cell state.
- **Encoder-decoder recurrence:** encodes one sequence and autoregressively
  generates another, often with attention.

## Interview Questions

- Why are shared parameters across time important in an RNN?
- Derive the recurrent Jacobian product that causes vanishing gradients.
- Why can gradient clipping help explosion but not vanishing?
- What is the difference between an LSTM's cell state and hidden state?
- Explain the forget, input, and output gates without using their names.
- Why does an additive cell update improve gradient flow?
- Does an LSTM eliminate vanishing gradients?
- Derive the LSTM parameter count.
- What does truncated BPTT change mathematically?
- Why are RNNs difficult to parallelize across sequence positions?
- When might an LSTM be preferable to a Transformer?
- Compare an LSTM gate with a SwiGLU gate.
